title: This Custom of Customs
summary: Josh and Chuck open with banter about Josh wearing shorts, then a long tangent on darts (501 and cricket). The main topic is customs: what customs agencies do, their origins under Alexander Hamilton and the early US Congress, tariffs and duties as revenue, the Customs Service's role in funding expansion (Louisiana Purchase, Alaska), its spoils system and famous employees Nathaniel Hawthorne and Herman Melville, and its role in Prohibition-era rum running. They discuss the Safe Ports Act and container scanning, the traveler declaration process, the $800 duty exemption and its variations, duty-free shops and alcohol and tobacco allowances, and banned or restricted items such as absinthe, dog and cat products, and animal-hide drums. They also cover drug smuggling interdiction, detection methods, produce and pest inspections in California (Mediterranean fruit fly), the Johnny Depp dog quarantine incident, cultural artifact repatriation, and ICE versus CBP. The episode ends with a listener email about missing and murdered Indigenous women in British Columbia, and the usual sign-off.

segments.title: Opening banter: shorts and darts
segments.summary: Josh wears shorts to the office, and the hosts riff on it. Josh describes the darts game 501 and cricket and says he used to play in leagues.

segments.title: What customs is and why tariffs exist
segments.summary: The hosts explain customs as the government agency that regulates imports and exports, and that customs and immigration were merged under Homeland Security in 2003. They describe duties and tariffs as taxes on trade, using a potato example to show how tariffs protect domestic producers.

segments.title: Origins of US Customs under Hamilton
segments.summary: Alexander Hamilton proposed tariffs on imports as federal revenue to pay Revolutionary War debts and fund government. The first Congress created the Customs Service shortly after the Constitution was ratified. For much of US history it was the largest agency and top revenue source until the IRS took over that role.

segments.title: Customs revenue, expansion, and spinoff agencies
segments.summary: Customs tariff money helped fund infrastructure, lighthouses, and territorial expansion, including the Louisiana Purchase and Alaska. The agency also housed functions later split into separate agencies such as immigration, the Coast Guard, Border Patrol, and the DEA.

segments.title: Spoils system and famous customs employees
segments.summary: The hosts describe the Customs Service's patronage spoils system. Nathaniel Hawthorne worked as a weigher at the Boston Custom House, and Herman Melville also got a customs job, which the museum credits with helping him recover from depression.

segments.title: Prohibition, rum running, and customs danger
segments.summary: The hosts say customs work was dangerous and bribery was common during Prohibition. Rum runners used faster boats and mother ships offshore, which the hosts link to the origins of speedboats and the fast-car culture of NASCAR.

segments.title: Container scanning and the Safe Ports Act
segments.summary: The Safe Ports Act of 2006 called for scanning a share of shipping containers entering US ports, a target that was not met by its deadlines. Industry groups argue scanning would slow trade. Alternatives such as electronic seals and international weighing rules are discussed.

segments.title: Traveler declarations and the duty exemption
segments.summary: Travelers must declare purchases and repairs made abroad. The duty exemption is generally $800, up to $1,600 in insular possessions such as Guam, and families can combine exemptions. Duty is small above the exemption. Alcohol and tobacco limits are discussed.

segments.title: Duty free shops and airplane sales
segments.summary: The hosts complain about duty free shops and whether their prices are really better. They note that duty free means exempt for the store owner, and that in-flight sales and credit card pitches annoy them. They also discuss airline fees.

segments.title: Banned and restricted imports
segments.summary: Examples include absinthe, whose labeling rules limit the brand name and imagery. Products made from dog or cat are banned as of 2000. Animal-hide drums from Haiti may be restricted due to anthrax risk, which connects to a Mental Floss article and an old TV show episode.

segments.title: Drug smuggling interdiction and detection
segments.summary: Customs works with the DEA, Coast Guard, and others to stop drug smuggling, using radar planes, helicopters, and boat chases. Agents can search travelers without a warrant. Detection methods include sniffer devices, drug dogs, and X-ray. The hosts describe body-packing cases and cash reporting rules.

segments.title: Agricultural inspections and Johnny Depp quarantine
segments.summary: Produce and plant checks at state lines and borders target pests. The hosts recall the Mediterranean fruit fly outbreaks in California in the 1980s and a disputed claim about eco-terrorists. They also discuss Johnny Depp and Amber Heard bringing dogs into Australia without quarantine.

segments.title: Cultural artifacts and ICE
segments.summary: Cultural artifacts are regulated and looted items are returned. The hosts distinguish ICE from CBP and give a short TV aside.

segments.title: Listener mail: missing Indigenous women in BC
segments.summary: A listener from Montreal writes about the disappearance and murder of Indigenous women in British Columbia, and links it to the hosts' earlier episode on the mysterious feet. She recommends the documentary Highway of Tears.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts give social media and contact information and sign off.
